President of the United States, Mr. Donald J. Trump, on the sidelines 
of the G7 Summit in Évian, France, on 17 June 2026. 
PM  raised  the  issue  of  safety  of  Indian  maritime  workers  and 
sailors, both during his bilateral meeting with President Trump and  
during his intervention at the G7 Summit Outreach Session on 16  
June 2026. He highlighted that the ongoing conflict in West Asia had 
disrupted global maritime trade through the Strait of  Hormuz and  
resulted in the loss of lives, including those of Indian seafarers. He  
emphasized the importance of  maintaining freedom of  navigation  
and unimpeded commerce through the Strait, while underscoring  
that the safety and security of  seafarers who make a significant  
contribution  to  global  maritime  trade,  should  remain  a  shared 
concern of the international community.

3
Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the  
India-U.S.  Comprehensive  Global  Strategic  Partnership  and  
welcomed  the  progress  made  under  the  India-U.S.  COMPACT 
(Catalyzing  Opportunities  for  Military  Partnership,  Accelerated 
Commerce  and  Technology),  including  in  the  areas  of  defence, 
strategic technologies, energy and bilateral trade. They noted with  
satisfaction  the  significant  progress  in  negotiations  towards  an 
interim Bilateral  Trade  Agreement  and directed  their  officials  to 
work towards an early conclusion of a balanced, mutually beneficial  
and commercially meaningful agreement.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
DEPARTMENT OF FERTILIZERS 
 
LOK SABHA 
 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 976 TO BE ANSWERED ON: 24.07.2026 
 
Availability of Fertilizers in Haryana 
 
976. Shri Deepender Singh Hooda:          
 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 
(a) the details of the requirement, allocation, supply and utilisation of DAP and Urea in 
Haryana during the last ten years, district-wise and year-wise; 
 
(b) whether the Government considers that the quantity supplied to meet the 
requirements of farmers in Haryana is sufficient, if so, the details thereof; 
 
(c) if not, the reasons for shorter supply and the corrective measures taken to ensure 
timely and adequate supply of DAP and Urea to farmers in the State; 
 
  (d) the details of imports of DAP and Urea during the last ten years, including the 
quantity imported from each country, country-wise and year-wise; and 
 
  (e) the steps taken by the Government to increase indigenous production of DAP and 
Urea so as to reduce dependence on imports? 
 
ANSWER 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS 
 
(SMT. ANUPRIYA PATEL) 
 
(a) to (c) Following steps are taken by the Government every season for ensuring 
timely and adequate supply of fertilizers in the country, including the State of Haryana: 
i. Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture and 
Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, assesses 
the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers.  
ii. On the basis of requirement projected by DA&FW, D/o Fertilizers allocates adequate 
quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and continuously 
monitors the availability. 
 
 

-2- 
iii. The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the country 
by an on-line web based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer Management 
System (iFMS). 
iv. Regular Weekly Video Conference is conducted jointly by DA&FW and D/o 
Fertilizers with State Agriculture Officials and corrective actions are taken to dispatch 
fertilizers as indicated by the State Governments. 
 
Further, the distribution of fertilizers within the State at district level is done by the State 
Government. Accordingly, as per the information received from the State Government 
of Haryana, the information regarding requirement, receipt and sales of Urea and DAP 
in the districts of Haryana during the last 10 years is placed at Annexure-A. 
Moreover, the availability of Urea and DAP has remained adequate in the State of 
Haryana during the ongoing Kharif 2026 season as shown under:

(d) The details regarding the imports of Urea and DAP for the last 10 years, 
including the current financial year up to June, along with the country-wise details, are 
placed at Annexure-B. 
(e) The Government implemented the Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Scheme for 
Phosphatic and Potassic (P&K) fertilizers with effect from 1st April 2010. Under the 
Scheme, P&K fertilizers are covered under the Open General License (OGL), allowing 
companies to import or manufacture these fertilizers based on their business 
requirements and market dynamics. 
To reduce dependence on imported phosphatic fertilizers and promote self-reliance, 
the Government has undertaken several measures to encourage domestic production. 
The Guidelines dated 18th January 2024 on the reasonableness of Maximum Retail 
Price (MRP) provide for reasonable profit margins of 8-10% for 
importers/manufacturers and 12% for integrated manufacturers. Based on requests  

-3- 
received, new manufacturing units and expansions in the production capacity of 
existing units have been recognized and taken on record under the NBS Scheme. 
Additionally, the number of P&K fertilizer grades covered under the Scheme has 
increased from 22 in 2021 to 28 at present. To promote the use of Single Super 
Phosphate (SSP), an indigenously manufactured fertilizer, freight subsidy has been 
provided since the Kharif season of 2022, thereby encouraging the application of 
phosphatic (P) nutrients to the soil. Furthermore, the nutrient-wise subsidy rates under 
the NBS Scheme are revised on a biannual basis to ensure the adequate availability 
of fertilizers under the Scheme. 
With regard to Urea, the Government had announced New Investment Policy (NIP) – 
2012 on 2nd January, 2013 and its amendment on 7th October, 2014 to facilitate fresh 
investment in the urea sector and to make India self-sufficient in the urea sector. Total 
6 new urea units have been set up under NIP-2012 which includes 4 urea units set up 
through Joint Venture Companies (JVC) of nominated PSUs and 2 urea units set up 
by the private companies. The units set up through JVC are Ramagundam urea unit 
of Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL) in Telangana and 3 urea units 
namely Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni of Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan Limited 
(HURL) in Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Bihar, respectively. The units set up by 
private companies are Panagarh urea unit of Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. 
(Matix) in West Bengal; and Gadepan-III urea unit of Chambal Fertilizers and 
Chemicals Ltd. (CFCL) in Rajasthan. Each of these units has installed capacity of 12.7 
Lakh Metric Tonne per annum (LMTPA). These units are highly energy efficient as 
they are based on latest technology. Therefore, these units have together added urea 
production capacity of 76.2 LMTPA, thereby total indigenous urea production capacity 
(Reassessed Capacity, RAC) has increased from 207.54 LMTPA during 2014-15 to 
269.42 LMTPA during 2026-27. Further, an exclusive policy for the revival of Talcher 
unit of FCIL through JVC of nominated PSUs namely Talcher Fertilizers Limited (TFL) 
by setting up a new Greenfield Urea plant of 12.7 LMTPA at coal gasification route 
has also been approved. Further, setting up of a new Brownfield Ammonia-Urea 
Complex named as Assam Valley Fertilizer and Chemical Company Ltd. (AVFCCL) 
with an annual capacity of 12.7 Lakh Metric Tonne of Urea through Joint Venture within 
the existing premises of Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Limited (BVFCL), 
Assam has been approved. These two projects are under execution phase. 
Also, the Government had notified the New Urea Policy (NUP) – 2015 on 25th May, 
2015 for the existing 25 gas-based urea units with one of the objectives of maximizing 
indigenous urea production beyond RAC.  The NUP-2015 has led to additional 
production of urea by 20-25 LMT as compared to the production during 2014-15 
annually.  
Above steps together have facilitated increase of Urea production from level of 225 
LMT per annum during 2014-15 to a record Urea Production at 314.07 LMT during 
2023-24. During 2025-26, 293.30 LMT of Urea was produced in the country. 
 
 

-4- 
In addition to this, on 15.07.2026, CCEA approved National Investment Policy for 
Urea-2026 for Aatmanirbhar Bharat (NIPU-2026) for making fresh investments in Urea 
Sector. 
Besides, as informed by the State Government of Haryana, State Agriculture 
Department has promoted the judicious and balanced use of fertilizers. The 
Department has also undertaken several statewide awareness initiatives, including 
Special Awareness Campaigns, Khet Bachao Abhiyan, and Dharti Mata Bachao 
Abhiyan. Through these campaigns, farmers have been sensitized for balanced 
nutrient application, soil health management, and the efficient use of chemical 
fertilizers, thereby encouraging sustainable agricultural practices across the State.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF PORTS, SHIPPING AND WATERWAYS

977.    DR. ALOK KUMAR SUMAN: 
 
      Will the Minister of PORTS, SHIPPING AND WATERWAYS be pleased to state:

(a) whether the Government has implemented inland waterway projects during the last 
three years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof along with the status of projects on National Waterway-1 
passing through Bihar; 
(c) whether the Government has taken measures to promote inland cargo movement 
and if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether the Government has proposed additional river terminals for development 
in Bihar and if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the details of steps taken by the Government to modernize inland water transport 
infrastructure in the country?  
  
  
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF PORTS, SHIPPING AND WATERWAYS 
(SHRI SARBANANDA SONOWAL)  
  
(a), (b) and (d) Yes. The details of inland waterway projects implemented during the 
last three years along with its status on National Waterway (NW) -l, including the 
projects in Bihar are given at Annexure-I.   
(c) Infrastructure and Policy measures taken by the Government to promote inland 
cargo movement on NWs are detailed at Annexure-II. 
 (e) The Government has embarked upon a transformational drive to promote inland 
waterways as a key pillar of India's multimodal transport system under, Maritime India 
Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047. The Inland Water Transport (IWT) 
development in India encompass creation of World-class waterway infrastructure 
through fairway development, development of multimodal terminals, community 
jetties, river cruise terminals, establishment of Regional Centres of Excellence, 
promoting digital navigation and adoption of Green vessel technologies, coupled with 
seamless integration under the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan. 
  

  To improve Ease of Doing Business, digital initiatives including Portal for Asset 
and navigation Information (PANI), Jalyan & Navic portal, Cargo data portal (CAR-D), 
Jal Samriddhi portal, digital hydrographic surveys charts etc. have been introduced by 
Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), an autonomous organization  under the 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways to simplify approvals, enhance navigational 
safety and enable real-time information services to stakeholders.  
  
  The development of waterway infrastructure, digital and policy reforms have 
resulted in the operationalization of 32 NWs in the country and laying the foundation 
for a modern, technology-driven, sustainable and globally competitive IWT ecosystem 
that reduces logistics costs, promotes green mobility and accelerates inclusive 
economic growth.

strengthen cruise tourism and passenger movement on NW-2. 
4. Development of RCoE at Dibrugarh – Being developed at a cost of Rs. 188 
crore to provide training, skill development, and research infrastructure for the 
inland waterways sector. 
5. Construction of Steel Gangway with Yoke System at Pandu – Being 
developed at a cost of Rs. 2.88 crore to improve passenger and cargo 
accessibility and enhance vessel berthing operations at Pandu Terminal. 
6. Construction of Building for Regional Office, MSDC, Guest House and 
Office Space for ITAT at Fancy Bazar – Being developed at a cost of Rs. 
50.00 crore to strengthen administrative and skill development infrastructure for 
inland waterways operations. 
7. Link Road Connecting Pandu Terminal with Ship Repair Facility – Being 
developed at a cost of Rs. 55 crore to provide seamless connectivity for 
movement of heavy machinery, vessels, and logistics equipment. 

8. Construction of 02 Nos. Steel Pontoons for Brahmaputra River (NW-2) – 
Being developed at a cost of Rs. 3.40 crore to improve floating terminal 
infrastructure and berthing operations on NW-2. 
9. Construction of 02 Nos. SDB Vessels for Brahmaputra River (NW-2) – 
Being constructed at a cost of Rs. 2.88 crore to strengthen inland passenger 
transportation and river connectivity on NW-2. 
10. Mathematical Modelling of Bogibeel Approach Channel – Being undertaken 
at a cost of Rs. 0.60 crore to improve fairway planning, navigational safety, and 
terminal sustainability at Bogibeel. 
11. DPR for Construction of Community Jetties – Being prepared at a cost of 
Rs. 5.56 crore to improve rural river connectivity and support safe passenger 
movement in remote riverine areas of Assam.  
 3.  Projects of Other NWs in the Country: 
(i) Kerala NWs: 
 Continued development of fairway channel on NW-3, NW-8 & NW-9 in the state 
of Kerala. 
 IWAI entrusted the works of re-construction of new Navigation lock at 
Thrikunnapuzha and single lane bridge at Kovilthottam in NW-3, to Government 
of Kerala on deposit basis. 
 NW-8 & NW-9 are connected to NW-3 at Alappuzha & both the NWs are 
operational (partly) for tourism & passenger movements. Provided 24 Hours 
navigational aids - 15 nos in NW-8 & 25 nos in NW-9 respectively for safe 
movement of tourism & passenger traffic round the clock. 4 nos. HDPE Jetties 
being installed at feasible locations in NW-3. 
(ii) Andhra Pradesh & Telangana NWs: 
 Land acquisition completed at Muktyala and Harichandrapuram. Land 
acquisition under progress at Ibrahimpatnam through the Govt. of Andhra 
Pradesh in NW-4. 
 Ro-Ro terminal development is undertaken at Muktyala, Harischandrapuram 
along with its associated infrastructure. 
 4 nos. steel floating Pontoon Jetty handed over to Andhra Pradesh Tourism 
Development corporation (APTDC) under State Support Agreement (SSA) for 
promotion of tourism activities. 
 03 steel floating pontoon jetties  under fabrication for installation in Krishna 
River (NW-4) portion of Telangana State. 
(iii) Odisha NWs: 
 Regular longitudinal thalweg survey being undertaken in Odisha NWs. 
 10  navigational buoys were installed in Mahanadi River (NW-64) for safe 
movement of the cargo vessel. 

 Developing of Talcher- Dhamra- Paradip Port stretches of NW-5 towards 
evacuation of the coal movement from Talcher in Odisha. 
 3  concrete jetties being installed in NW-14 & NW-64 for promotion of tourism 
activities.  
(iv) Karnataka NWs: 
 Development of Kabini River (NW-51) and Sharavati River (NW-90) for river 
cruise tourism. 
 03 concrete Jetties being installed in Kabini River and Sharavati River for 
promotion of tourism activities.  
(v) Goa NWs: 
 Development of Mandovi River, Zuari River and Cumberjua River for river 
cruise tourism in Goa. 
 10 concrete jetties being installed on Mandovi River, Zuari River and 
Cumberjua River for promotion of tourism activities.  
(vi) UT of J&K NWs: 
 Action initiated for undertaking developmental works such as on-shore facilities, 
floating concrete Jetties and navigational aids in Jhelum River (NW-49), 
Chenab River (NW-26) and Ravi River (NW-84). 
(vii) Himachal Pradesh & Punjab NWs: 
 Feasibility study in Beas River (NW-17) and Sutlej River (NW-98) is being 
undertaken. 
(viii) Gujarat NWs: 
 Developmental activities undertaken in Narmada River (NW-73) and Tapi River 
(NW-100) for river cruise tourism. 
 02  floating concrete jetties installed in Narmada River (NW-73) & 02  floating 
concrete jetties being installed in Tapi River (NW-100) for promotion of tourism 
activities. 
(ix) West Bengal NWs: 
 Developmental activities undertaken in Ichamati River (NW-44) and Sundarban 
Waterways (NW-97). 
 Single lane bridge at Swaroopnagar which was obstruction for safe navigation 
across Ichamati River (NW-44) completed in March, 2026 and was inaugurated 
by the Hon’ble PM. 
 Sundarban Waterways from Silvertree point to Atharabanki (201 Km) 
comprises of an international IWT route, which provided International 
connectivity with Bangladesh and North Eastern states of India forms part of 
Indo-Bangladesh Protocol route 1,2 and 3,4 under Protocol on Inland Water 
Transit and Trade (PIWTT) between India and Bangladesh. 

4.  Hydrographic Survey Projects in National Waterways:  
(i) Hydrographic Survey in NWs: 
At present, regular weekly/ fortnightly/ monthly thalweg surveys are being carried out 
in 22 National Waterways, namely NW-1, NW-2, NW-3, NW-4, NW-5, NW-8, NW-9, 
NW-14, NW-16, NW-23, NW-31, NW-40, NW-44, NW-47, NW-57, NW-64, NW-73, 
NW-86, NW-94, NW-97, NW-100, NW-110, and the Indo-Bangladesh Protocol (IBP) 
route. 
This expansion reflects a significant enhancement in the hydrographic monitoring 
network to ensure regular assessment of navigational channels, maintenance of 
fairway conditions and improved safety and reliability of inland water transport 
operations. 
(ii).   River Information Service System 
IWAI implemented the River Information Service (RIS) system on NW-1 (Ganga River) 
in three phases during the period from 2015 to 2020, covering the stretches of Phase-
I: Haldia–Farakka, Phase-II: Farakka–Patna and Phase-III: Patna–Varanasi. 
The RIS system comprises 4 Control Stations and 13 Base Stations equipped with 
advanced communication and monitoring infrastructure including Automatic 
Identification System (AIS), VHF communication systems, servers, monopole towers, 
meteorological sensors and other associated equipment. The system facilitates real-
time tracking and monitoring of vessels plying on the waterway enabling enhanced 
navigational safety, efficient traffic management and improved operational efficiency 
of inland water transport. 
Further, 30 departmental vessels have been equipped with RIS consoles to provide 
necessary navigational assistance to vessel masters during their operations on NW-
1. 
(iii).   Electronic Navigational Charts (ENC)  
IWAI has prepared ENCs for operational and tidal NWs for providing detailed 
information to the Mariners for navigation of vessels plying in the NW-1, NW-3, NW-5, 
NW-8, NW-9, NW-10, NW-14, NW-23, NW-27, NW-53, NW-64, NW-68, NW-73, NW-
83, NW-86, NW-91, NW-110 and NW-111 and are uploaded on IWAI Vessel Tracker 
& PANI. Prior to 2014, ENCs were available only for NW-1.  
  
 
 
 
 
 
 

Annexure-II 
 
Measures taken by the Government to promote inland cargo movement on NW  
  
1. Infrastructure measures:  
  
(i) 66 community jetties, 20 floating terminals, 3 Multi-Modal Terminals (MMT), 1 Inter-
Modal Terminal (IMT) and 4 Ro-Pax terminals have been constructed on NW-1 in 
addition to 5 pre-existing permanent terminals. 
  
(ii) 13 floating terminals provided on NW-2 along with MMTs at Pandu, Jogighopa and 
terminals at Bogibeel and Dhubri. Four dedicated Jetties for cruise vessels have been 
provided at Jogighopa, Pandu, Biswanath Ghat and Neamati. In addition to this, Jetties 
for cruise and passengers have been constructed at Sadiya, Lyka and Orium Ghat in 
Assam. 
  
(iii) 2 existing terminals at Badarpur & Karimganj on NW-16 have been upgraded/ 
renovated and 1 terminal at Sonamura on Gumati River in Tripura on IBP route has 
been constructed. 
  
(iv) 9 Permanent IWT terminals with godowns and 2 Ro-Ro/Ro-Pax terminals have 
been constructed on NW-3 in Kerala. 
  
(v) 4 floating concrete jetties have been provided to Govt. of Goa and installed on NW-
68. 
  
(vi) 4 Tourist Jetties on NW-4 in Andhra Pradesh have been commissioned and 8 
Floating Jetties on NW-110 in Mathura-Vrindavan stretch in Uttar Pradesh, 2 Jetties 
on NW-73  and 2 Jetties on NW-37 in Bihar have been established. 
  
(vii) A new Navigation Lock at Farakka has been constructed.  
  
(viii) 2 Quick Pontoon Opening Mechanisms (QPOMs) have been constructed on NW-
1 to facilitate smooth and faster movement of vessels. 
  
(ix) Fairway maintenance works (river training, maintenance dredging, channel 
marking and regular hydrographic surveys) have been taken up in various National 
Waterways for providing a navigation channel of 35/45 m width and 2.0 / 2.2 / 2.5 / 3.0 
m least available depth (LAD) for operation of vessels. 
  
2. Policy Measures: 
  
 Jalvahak Scheme: A scheme for providing 35% incentive to promote the 
utilization of inland waterways transport sector by cargo owners and for 
scheduled service for cargo movement on NW-1 and NW-2 and NW-16 
via IBP route by Inland & Coastal Shipping Limited (ICSL) has been approved 

by the Government.  The scheme is implemented at a cost of INR 95.42 Crore 
for three years.  
 Tonnage tax: An extension of the tonnage tax scheme to inland vessels 
registered under the Indian Vessels Act, 2021 was announced during the 
budget presented on 01.02.2025. Inland vessels operating on NWs, rivers, and 
canals, will be benefited. This move is expected to boost the industry's 
competitiveness and encourage more cargo owners to use inland waterways 
for transportation. A tonnage tax system is a special taxation policy for shipping 
companies where tax is not based on actual profits but on the size (tonnage) of 
the vessel. It provides stable, predictable, and lower taxation for vessel owners, 
reducing their financial burden.   
 The National Waterways (Construction of Jetties / Terminals) Regulations 
2025 has been notified, allowing private companies to invest and operate 
Inland Waterways infrastructure by providing a clear regulatory framework to 
attract private sector investment for facilitating the growth of inland waterways 
sector.  
 Jalyan & Navic : To increase ease of doing business in the IWT sector, along 
the same lines as ‘vahan’ and ‘sarathi’, a central data base and portal has been 
developed for registration of vessels and crew all over the country. This will 
facilitate registration of vessels and crew digitally and would also provide 
accurate status on number of vessels and crew in the country and thus help in 
planning.  
 Cargo Aggregation : The cargo movement on the waterways suffer from 
problems of multimodality because of lack of industries along the waterways. 
Therefore, projects for development of cargo aggregation hub – MMLP at 
Varanasi and Integrated Cluster- cum-Logistics Park, Sahibganj have been 
taken up. NHLML, a PSU under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
has been engaged for development of these MMLPs. The work of Rail 
connectivity for three MMTs has been assigned to M/s Indian Port and Rail 
Company Ltd. (a PSU under MoPSW).   
 Shift of cargo by PSUs: For modal shift of cargo to waterways, more than 140 
PSUs have been approached to plan their movement using IWT mode. They 
have been requested to outline their current status of cargo movement through 
the waterways and their plan for modal shift of cargo. Ministries of PNG, Co-
operation, Fertiliser, Food & Public Distribution, Heavy industries, Steel and 
Coal have been requested to advise the PSUs under their jurisdiction to utilise 
IWT mode as far as possible and earmark certain percentage of their cargo for 
IWT mode keeping in line the MIV targets.

Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state:

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
  
LOK SABHA 
 UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 979 
ANSWERED ON 24.07.2026 
  
PROGRESS OF MISSION VATSALYA 
 
979. DR. BYREDDY SHABARI: 
 SHRI APPALANAIDU KALISETTI: 
  
 Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
  
(a)     the details of the sanctioned and operational District Child Protection Units (DCPUs), Child 
Welfare Committees (CWCs) and Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs), State -wise and district -
wise, especially in Andhra Pradesh; 
(b)    the current status of the integrated Mission Vatsalya Portal; 
(c)     the details of the States/UTs participating in the Mission Vatsalya Portal; 
(d)    the number of States/UTs regularly uploading data on the said Portal, along with the criteria 
prescribed for regular data updation; 
(e)    whether the migration mapping of data from TrackChild, CARINGS, and Khoya -Paya have 
been completed to ensure a unified digital platform and if so, the details thereof; and 
(f)     the number of operational Cradle Baby Reception Centres established in Specialized 
Adoption Agencies (SAAs) to rescue abandoned children, State -wise and district -wise, 
especially in the said State? 
  
ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR) 
  
(a): The Mission Vatsalya Scheme is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, which is implemented by 
the States and Union Territories (UTs) with the aim to support Children in Need of care and 
Protection (CNCP) and Children in Conflict with Law (CCL). Under the Missi on Vatsalya 
Scheme, financial assistance is provided to the States and Union Territories for supporting the 
statutory service delivery structures established under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection 
of Children) Act, 2015, including District Child P rotection Units (DCPUs), Child Welfare 
Committees (CWCs) and Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs). The State-wise details of DCPUs, CWCs 
and JJBs, including those in Andhra Pradesh funded under Mission Vatsalya Scheme, are placed 
at Annexure-I. 

 (b) to (e): The Ministry of Women and Child Development has developed an integrated unified 
Mission Vatsalya Portal in consultation and coordination with States and UTs.  The TrackChild 
portal for Missing/Found Children, and Khoya -Paya application for Missing/Sighted Children 
have been integrated with this unified Mission Vatsalya Portal. The Portal integrates key child 
protection services and facilitates digital case management, benefic iary tracking, institutional 
monitoring and reporting by States and UTs. The Portal also integrates the Child Adoption 
Resource Information and Guidance System (CARINGS) portal thereby strengthening tracking, 
rehabilitation and adoption-related services for children in need of care and protection.  
  
The Mission Vatsalya Portal has been rolled out across all 36 States and Union Territories. States 
and Union Territories, have been advised from time to time to ensure regular updation of child -
specific and institutional data. Data is updated by authorised  users, including District Child 
Protection Units (DCPUs), Child Welfare Committees (CWCs), Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs), 
Child Care Institutions (CCIs) and Specialized Adoption Agencies (SAAs), in accordance with the 
Mission Vatsalya Operational Guideli nes and the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) issued 
by the Ministry. 
  
The Ministry regularly monitors the quality, completeness and timeliness of data through periodic 
review meetings, capacity -building programmes and advisories issued to the States and Union 
Territories. 
   
(f): There is provision in Mission Vatsalya Guidelines for the establishment of at least one Cradle 
Baby Reception Centre (CBRC) in a Specialized Adoption Agency (SAA) in each district. CBRCs 
are operated from the premises of the SAAs and are equipped with  essential facilities for the 
immediate care and protection of infants.  
  
The State -wise details of Specialized Adoption Agencies (SAAs) funded under the Mission 
Vatsalya Scheme, including those in Andhra Pradesh, are provided at Annexure-II.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
  
 LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 980 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 24.07.2026 
  
Implementation of the One Stop Centre Scheme for Women 
  
980. Smt. Smita Uday Wagh: 
  
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
  
(a) whether the Government is implementing the One Stop Centre (OSC) Scheme to provide 
integrated support services to women affected by violence and distress, if so, the details thereof; 
  
(b) the details of the operational One Stop Centres, beneficiaries assisted, services provided State 
and district-wise particularly for Maharashtra, including Jalgaon Lok Sabha Constituency; 
  
(c) whether the Government has assessed the effectiveness of OSCs in providing emergency 
assistance, temporary shelter, legal aid, medical care and psychological counselling, if so, the 
details thereof; 
  
(d) whether the Government has reviewed accessibility, staffing infrastructure gaps in OSCs 
functioning in rural and semi -urban areas of said State, including said Constituency, if so, the 
details thereof; and 
  
(e) whether the Government proposes to strengthen OSC services through enhanced counselling, digital 
support and trained personnel in the said Constituency, if so, the details thereof? 
  
ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR) 
  
  
(a) to (e):    One Stop Centre (OSC) is a component of the Sambal vertical under the umbrella 
Mission Shakti. It provides integrated and immediate support and assistance under one roof to 
women affected by violence and those in distress, both in private and public spa ces. It provides 
services like medical aid, legal aid and advice, temporary shelter, police assistance and psycho -
social counselling to needy women including rural and semi-urban areas of country. As on date, 
985 One Stop Centres have been made operational across the country and since inception, i.e. 1st 
April, 2015 to 30th June, 2026, over 15.20 lakh women have been assisted in the country. As on 

date, 68 OSCs are operational in the State of Maharashtra including one OSC in Jalgaon district. 
Over 47,523 women have been assisted through these OSCs in Maharashtra including Jalgaon 
Lok Sabha Constituency.  State and UT-wise details of operational One Stop Centre and women 
beneficiaries assisted through One Stop Centre have been placed at  Annexure. 
As per the Mission Shakti guidelines, the Central Government provides 100% financial assistance 
to States and UTs under Sambal sub -scheme. Adequate staff and infrastructural support is 
provided for smooth operationalization of OSCs across the country. Howe ver, the 
implementation of the all schemes under Mission Shakti lies with the State Governments and UT 
Administrations. 
The Ministry has taken keen action in standardizing capacity building sessions for the functionaries of One 
Stop Centres. This involves engaging expert resource persons from NIMHANS, UNFPA, SPNIWCD, 
NALSA, and National Informatics Centre for facilitating technical sessions on psycho-social counselling, 
gender-based violence case management, gender sensitization and dashboard operations. 
  
Further, once in a year, the Programme Approval Board (PAB) monitors with States and UTs the progress 
of activities under the scheme and reviews status of achievement of objectives, effective delivery of services 
to women and children.  Apart from this, officials of the Ministry continuously review the scheme through 
meetings, video conferencing and by making field visits to States/UTs from time to time. The Ministry has 
also developed the Mission Shakti Dashboard, which facilitates real -time tracking of functioning of the 
Schemes under the Mission Shakti at the district, State, and National levels. 
Two third party evaluations of the schemes of the Ministry, including the Mission Shakti 
Umbrella Scheme have been conducted in 2020 and again in 2025 through NITI Aayog. The 
studies have found the relevance, effectiveness and sustainability of the scheme as satisfactory.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENTOF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 981
TO BE ANSWERED ON 24TH JULY,2026
MARKET ACCESS PROGRAMMES BY PHARMA COMPANIES
981. SHRI K C VENUGOPAL:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the details of guidelines governing the conduct of market access and patient assistance
programmes by pharmaceutical companies in private hospitals;
(b) the institutional mechanisms in place to monitor these programmes, the use of patient data
and the outcomes generated therefrom, along with the specific role played by the State Health
Departments in this regard; and
(c) the measures taken by the Government to ensure that pharmaceutical companies do not
influence the pricing mechanisms or the inclusion of high-end drugs and diagnostics in the
benefit packages of Central and State health insurance schemes?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA)
(a) & (b): As informed by Department of Pharmaceuticals (DoP), the pharmaceutical
companies implement Patient Assistance Programmes (PAPs)/Market Access Programmes as
voluntary initiatives to improve patient access and affordability of innovative medicines.
These programmes are administered through independent third-party agencies based on
defined patient eligibility criteria and company-specific operating procedures, with
appropriate safeguards, including oversight mechanisms, periodic audits and grievance
redressal systems.
As informed by Department of Pharmaceuticals (DoP), the pharmaceutical companies
have established internal oversight and control mechanisms for the implementation of PAPs,
including verification of patient eligibility and prescriptions, monitoring of third-party
agencies, confirmation of drug administration and periodic independent audits. Patient
information is collected and processed by the third-party agencies only for programme
administration and treatment continuity.

(c): As informed by Department of Pharmaceuticals (DoP), the National Pharmaceutical
Pricing Authority (NPPA) under the Department of Pharmaceuticals fixes ceiling prices of
formulations and medical devices included in the National List of Essential Medicines
published by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and incorporated by the DoP in
Schedule-I to the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 (DPCO, 2013). NPPA also fixes the
retail price of new drugs as defined in section 2(1) (u) of DPCO, 2013. In case of non-
scheduled formulations, manufacturers are required to not increase the maximum retail price
(MRP) of such formulations by more than 10% of MRP during preceding 12 months. NPPA
monitors the prices of both scheduled and non-scheduled formulations/medical devices and
takes action in accordance with the provisions of DPCO, 2013 against companies that are
found overcharging consumers.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF AYUSH 
 
LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 982 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 24.07.2026 
 
Promotion of AYUSH Systems and Traditional Medicines 
†982. Shri Jaswantsinh Sumanbhai Bhabhor: 
Will the Minister of AYUSH be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the specific steps taken by the Government to promote AYUSH systems, 
including Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy, at the grassroot level in the 
Dahod Parliamentary Constituency, stream-wise; 
(b) the efforts made to promote traditional AYUSH medicines and products from the tribal 
and rural areas of the Dahod Parliamentary Constituency; 
(c) the progress made so far in the implementation of the AYUSH Grid and 'My AYUSH 
Integrated Services Portal' in the Dahod Parliamentary Constituency, along with the extent of 
its adoption by health institutions in the Constituency; and 
(d) the measures taken by the Government to integrate AYUSH systems through co -location 
at Health and Wellness Centres in the Dahod Parliamentary Constituency and the impact this 
integration has had on preventive healthcare? 
 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (IC) OF THE MINISTRY OF AYUSH 
(SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHAV) 
 
(a) & (b) Public Health being a State Subject, primary responsibility regarding promotion of 
Ayush systems at the grassroot level  & promoting Ayush medicines and products from the 
tribal and rural areas including Dahod Parliamentary Constituency , lies with respective State 
Government. However, Ministry of Ayush is implementing the Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
of National Ayush Mission (NAM) through State/UT Governments and supporting their 
efforts for overall development and promotion of Ayush systems including Ayurveda, Yoga, 
Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy, in the country. Under NAM, grant -in-aid is being provided 
to the State /UT Governments against their proposals received through State Annual Action 
Plans (SAAPs) as per the provisions of NAM guidelines. The NAM inter -alia makes 
provision for following activities: 
 
(i) Operationalization of Ayush Health & Wellness Centres (AHWCs) , now renamed as 
Ayushman Arogya Mandir (Ayush). 

2 
 
(ii) Co -location of Ayush facilities at Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community 
Health Centres (CHCs) and District Hospitals (DHs) 
(iii) Upgradation of existing standalone Government Ayush Hospitals 
(iv) Upgradation of existing Government/Panchayat/Government aided Ayush 
Dispensaries/ Construction of building for existing Ayush Dispensary 
(Rented/dilapidated accommodation) /Construction of building to establish new Ayush 
Dispensary 
(v) Setting up of 10/30/50 bedded integrated Ayush Hospitals   
(vi) Supply of essential drugs to Government Ayush Hospitals, Government 
Dispensaries and Government/Government aided Teaching Institutional Ayush Hospitals 
(vii) Ayush Public Health Programs 
(viii) Ayush Gram 
(ix) Behavior Change Communication (BCC) 
(x) Establishment of new Ayush colleges in the States where availability of AYUSH 
teaching institutions is inadequate in Government Sector. 
(xi) Infrastructural development of Ayush Under -Graduate Institutions and Ayush Post -
Graduate Institutions/add on PG/ Pharmacy/Para-Medical Courses. 
 
Further, Ministry of Ayush is also implementing the Central Sector Scheme for 
Promotion of Information, Education and Communication (IEC) in Ayush to create 
awareness among the public about the efficacy, cost -effectiveness, and preventive healthcare 
benefits of the Ayush systems, namely Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, and Homoeopathy. 
The Scheme is intended to benefit all sections of the population across the country. Under the 
Scheme, the Ministry organises national and state -level Arogya Fairs, Yoga Fests/Utsavs, 
Ayurveda Parvs, and celebrations of important days associated with the various Ayush 
systems. It also participates in health fairs, melas, and exhibitions; provides financial 
assistance for organising seminars, workshops, and conferences; and conducts multimedia 
awareness campaigns to promote the Ayush systems of healthcare among citizens. 
As reported by the State Government of Gujarat, under the National Ayush Mission, 
robust financial and infrastructural support is extended to upgrade existing Ayush facilities 
across the Dahod Parliamentary C onstituency. In Dahod district, out of the 19 AYUSH 
dispensaries, 12 have been upgraded to Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AYUSH) . Further, 7 
Standalone AYUSH dispensaries , 2 Standalone Ayurvedic Hospitals having dedicated yoga 
wellness centres  and 5 Co-located Ayush OPDs ( 3 at CHCs, 1 a t PHC, and 1 at District 
Hospital level) are also functional in Dahod district . Regular and streamlined supply chains 
for essential Ayurvedic and Homoeopathic medicines have been institutionalized to cater 
directly to grass -roots Ayush dispensaries. For promotion of Ayush streams, activities like 
IEC (pamphlets, posters, and calendars highlighting Ayush benefits),  integration of herbal 
gardens, Ayush mobile medical unit, school health programs undertaken. Regular Yoga 
sessions for healthy lifestyle promotion, Health education and IEC activities on nutrition, 
hygiene, non-communicable disease prevention and seasonal health  are also done . Further, 

3 
 
Lifestyle counselling for diabetes, hypertension, obesity , stress management  and Ayush-
based preventive care for maternal and child health, adolescent health , geriatric care are also 
provided. Community outreach through health camps and observance of national health 
campaigns are also undertaken.  
 
Also, Gujarat Government implemented 'AYUSH Gram' activity to integrate 
traditional medicine into the daily lives of rural communities. These initiatives focus on 
making Ayush the primary, accessible healthcare system at the village level by training local 
attendants (like farmers), promoting local medicinal plants.  
 
   
(c) Under Ayush Grid initiative, twenty -four e -governance platforms have been developed 
and made accessible to all. The My Ayush Integrated Services Portal (MAISP), the master 
portal of the Ministry of Ayush, integrates all Ayush -related applications and services into a 
unified digital ecosystem. (Details available at: maisp.ayush.gov.in). As on 23rd July 2026, 3 
Ayush facilities have been on -boarded from Dahod parliamentary constituency and total of 
5558 Ayush health facilities across the country have been onboarded onto AHMIS. Further, 
the PM GatiShakti portal has enabled GIS mapping of Ayush health facilities using PM 
Gatishakti Ayush Asset Mapping Tool to support planning and decision -making. As on 23rd 
July 2026, a total of 34 Ayush facilities have been mapped from Dahod parliamentary 
constituency on the portal. 
 
(d) To integrate Ayush Systems with main -stream, Government of India has adopted a 
strategy of co -location of Ayush services with Primary Health Centers (PHCs), Community 
Health Centers (CHCs) and District Hospitals (DHs) across the country , thus enabling the 
choice to the patients for different systems of medicines under a single window. The 
engagement of Ayush doctors/ paramedics and their training is being supported by the 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare under National Health Mission (NHM), while the 
support for Ayush infrastructure, equipment/ furniture and medicines is being provided by the 
Ministry of Ayush under National Ayush Mission (NAM), as shared responsibilities.  
 
 Further, as reported by the State Government of Gujarat, to maximize grassroots reach 
and single-window patient care, 5 Co-located Ayush OPDs are located at 1 PHC, 3 CHCs and 
1 DH level in the Dahod Parliamentary Constituency . At these co-located facilities, Ayush 
Medical officers provide preventive, promotive and primary healthcare services, including 
Yoga & lifestyle counselling, health education, and Ayush treatment alongside routine 
healthcare services. The initiative has improved access to Ayush services, increased 
awareness of preventive healthcare, promoted healthy lifestyles, enabled early management 
of lifestyle diseases and strengthened preventive healthcare delivery, particularly in rural and 
tribal areas.

SAFETY MEASURES FOR HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS 
  
983. THIRU D M KATHIR ANAND: 
  
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the Government has undertaken a comprehensive review of safety protocols, 
governing industrial storage, transportation and handling of ammonia and other hazardous 
chemicals after the Tiruvallur ammonia leak in Tamil Nadu, if so, the details thereof;  
(b) the details of safety standards prescribed by the Government for refrigeration systems using 
ammonia, along with the mechanism for ensuring compliance by industrial establishments;  
(c) whether the  Government proposes mandatory installation of ammonia leak detectors, 
automatic alarm systems, water -curtain arrangements and real -time monitoring equipment in 
industries handling hazardous chemicals, if so, the details thereof;  
(d) whether the Government has examined gaps in enforcement of existing safety regulations 
and identified the corrective measures, if so, the details thereof; and  
(e) the time -bound action proposed by the Government to prevent recurrence of similar 
industrial disasters across the country, State-wise?  
  
ANSWER 
  
                  THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR CHEMICALS  & FERTILIZERS 
                  (SMT. ANUPRIYA PATEL)  
  
(a) to (e) The Central Government under the Ministry of labour and Employment has enacted 
the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH&WC) Code 2020, which has 
come into force on 21.11.2025, to regulate the occupational safety, health and working 
conditions of the persons employed in establishments including factories and for matters 
connected th erewith or incidental thereto. State /UT Government is the appropriate 
Government to implement the provisions of OSH&WC Code 2020 in case of factories. 

  
         The OSH&WC Code further, inter -alia, stipulates the duties of the employer to ensure 
that the  work place remains free from hazards that cause or are likely to cause injuries or 
occupational disease to the employees. 
  
        Further, as per information received from Director of Industrial Safety and Health, 
Government of Tamil Nadu, special teams  have been constituted to conduct inspections in 
factories handling Ammonia to ensure the safety of the workers. Instructions have also been 
issued to the officials to ensure that workers are not permitted to stay inside the factory premises 
where hazardous chemicals are handled or stored. As per these instructions, special squads 
have also been formed for conducting  inspections  in such  units handling Ammonia.

and capacity-building programmes for doctors, specialists, healthcare workers and other
stakeholders to ensure effective utilization of the platform.
Further, the platform enables consultations with specialist and super-specialist doctors and is
integrated with an AI-based Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) to support clinical

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 985
TO BE ANSWERED ON 24th JULY,2026
FOOD SAFETY ENFORCEMENT AGAINST ADULTERATION AND HARMFUL
ADDITIVES
985. MS KANGNA RANAUT:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFAREbe pleased to state:
(a) the number of inspections, food samples tested and prosecutions initiated by the Food
Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) against manufacturers of packaged food
products during the last three years;
(b) the number of cases in which food products were found to contain adulterants, excessive
preservatives, toxic contaminants or carcinogenic substances in excess of the prescribed limits;
(c) the action taken by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) against
defaulting manufacturers including product recalls, licence suspension or cancellation,
imposition of penalties and prosecution; and
(d) the measures taken by the Government to strengthen surveillance, laboratory testing and
consumer awareness regarding food safety standards across the country?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (d): Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is mandated to lay down
science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage,
distribution, sale and import to ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human
consumption. The implementation and enforcement of the Food Safety and Standards (FSS)
Act, 2006 is a shared responsibility between the Central and State Governments.
Around 98% of the Food Business Operators (FBOs) fall within the jurisdiction of the
State/UT Food Safety Authorities. To ensure compliance with the standards, limits, and other
statutory requirements prescribed under the FSS Act, 2006, and the regulations made
thereunder, the State Food Safety Authorities undertake surveillance, monitoring, targeted
enforcement drives, inspections, and sampling activities across the food sector.

Any deviation from the prescribed standards or violation of the provisions of the Food
Safety and Standards Regulation (FSSR), when detected, results in stringent regulatory and
punitive action against the non-compliant FBOs in accordance with the FSS Act, 2006 and the
rules framed thereunder, including suspension & cancellation of licence, prohibition on sale,
seizure & destruction of non-compliant food articles and judicial action through adjudication
(civil) and prosecution (criminal) as per the provisions outlined in Chapter IX (Offences and
Penalties) of FSS Act, 2006.
Total number of food recall in the FY 2024-25 was 754 and quantity of Food recall
was 51512.94 Kg. Total number of food recall in the FY 2025-26 was 1147 and quantity of
Food recall was 33540.68 Kg.
Details of the enforcement action taken viz., inspections, samples analysed, samples
found non-conforming including violations such as adulterants, excessive preservatives,
contaminants and penal action viz., adjudication & prosecution undertaken against the
defaulting FBOs including the manufacturers of packaged food products, for non-compliance
in the last 3 years is annexed at Annexure-I. The number of Licenses suspended and
cancelled in last 3 years is annexed at Annexure-II.
Measures taken to strengthen the laboratory testing, surveillance and consumer
awareness regarding food safety standards across the country are as:
 To ensure the safety of the food and food products through testing, FSSAI has
notified 259 National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories
(NABL) for analysis of food samples and 24 Referral Food Laboratories for the
analysis of appeal samples. These laboratories belong to the States/UTs, various
Government Institutions/Departments and private entities. FSSAI provides technical
and financial support to the State Food Safety Authorities, to strengthen the food
testing infrastructure in States & UTs. FSSAI has also provided assistance under the
scheme “Strengthening of Food Testing System in the Country including provision of
Mobile Food Testing Labs'' (SoFTeL) to various States and UTs.
 To strengthen the laboratory capacity, from 2017 to till date FSSAI has conducted 222
training programmes for its notified food testing laboratories in which 3937
participants have been trained.
 Mobile Food Testing Laboratory (MFTL) or “Food Safety on Wheels” (FSW) ensures
the widest outreach for food testing, training and awareness programme, especially in

the villages, towns and remote areas. Currently, 305 FSWs are deployed across 35
States/UTs.
 The "Magic Box" is a compact and user-friendly kit containing simple, rapid test
methods to detect common food adulterants in seven different food commodities. It
aims to identify adulteration in everyday food items such as milk, spices, oils, and
grains.
 Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test (DART) book covers 44 tests that can be
performed easily at household level with the help of water and simple solutions like
tincture of iodine for food products like Milk & Milk Products, Oils & Fats, Sugar &
Confectionary, Food Grains & its products, Spices & Condiments etc. These tests also
include sensory evaluation tests for establishing authentication of food products.
DART book depicts the differences between pure and adulterated food product
through pictorial representation.
 Rapid Analytical Food Testing (RAPID) Kits are advanced, easy to use, portable and
handheld devices and don't require any sophisticated equipment or conventional
reagents to conduct the tests. So far, 88 RAFT kits have been approved. These kits
help to reduce the screening time of the food products at the field level and thereby
accelerate surveillance as well as monitoring activities.
 The FSSAI also carries out a nation-wide movement 'Eat Right India' with a focus on
preventive and promotive healthcare through social and behavioural change through
State Food Safety Authorities. Financial assistance is provided to the States/UTs for
spreading consumer awareness.
 FSSAI has launched various campaigns such as “#No To Adulteration” to raise
consumer awareness about food adulteration and how to identify adulterated products.
These initiatives include advertisements, educational materials, and online platforms
to spread awareness.
 Videos “How to Check for Adulteration” on its official YouTube channel, which
includes short videos demonstrating methods to detect adulteration in various food
items, including milk and milk products, edible oil etc. These Information Education
Communication (IEC) materials are available in regional languages too and are
showcased at various public events and campaigns.
 Complaints/concerns of consumers and FBO are received through various channels
such as Web portal, Mobile App, FSSAI Helpline, State helpline, Twitter, Facebook,
etc. Complaints on Food Safety Connect Portal is part of the online Food Safety
Compliance System (FoSCoS). Complaints are attended by the respective State food

safety authorities and in cases, where the food samples are found non-conforming,
penal actions are initiated against the defaulting FBOs as per the provisions of FSS
Act, 2006, Rules and Regulations made thereunder.
 FSSAI is also carrying out an awareness campaign, "#HarLabelKuchKahtaHai", to
empower citizens with label literacy for healthier eating and informed choices. This
initiative educates consumers on key elements like nutritional information (calories,
fats, sugars, protein), ingredient lists, allergen warnings, and date markings.
******

“Implementation of Integrated ISO Standards” 
 
986.  Shri Biplab Kumar Deb: 
 
Will the Minister of AYUSH be pleased to state: 
 
(a)  whether the All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi has adopted any 
integrated management system to strengthen quality, safety and environmental 
compliance in its research laboratories; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof; 
(c)  the measures taken by the Government to standardise pre -clinical pharmacology 
research on ayurvedic formulations; and 
(d)  the impact of the adopting of ISO standards on research and laboratory efficiency? 
 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (IC) OF THE MINISTRY OF AYUSH 
(SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHA V) 
 
(a) & (b) The Pharmacology Laboratory of the All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), 
New Delhi has been accredited with Integrated Management System on 6th 
November 2025 by Bureau of Indian Standards to strengthen quality, safety and 
environmental compliance. 
The laboratory is accredited with :- 
• IS/ISO 9001:2015 QMS (Quality Management System),  
• IS/ISO 14001:2015 EMS (Environmental Management System), and  
• IS/ISO 45001:2018 OHSHS (Occupational Health and Safety Management 
System) 
  

Page 2 of 2 
 
 
 
 
(c) The measures taken by the AIIA  to standardize pre -clinical pharmacology 
research on Ayurvedic formulations are :- 
(i) Development and implementation of Standard Operating Procedures 
(SOPs) and Executive Procedures (EPs) for all laboratory activities, 
including, animal procurement, experimental protocols, bio -waste 
management, and reporting. 
(ii) Establishment of quality assurance mechanisms, internal audits and 
periodic reviews to maintain consistency in experimental outcomes. 
(iii) Use of validated protocols, and calibrated instruments to support 
accuracy and reliability in pre-clinical research. 
 
 
(d) The impact of adopting ISO standards on research outcomes and laboratory 
efficiency are :- 
(i) enhanced data reliability and reproducibility due to standardized 
processes and quality controls. 
(ii) improved environmental sustainability, resource optimization and waste 
management through Environmental Management System  
implementation. 
(iii) strengthened safety culture, reducing the risk of laboratory incidents and 
improving staff and scholars well-being.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
 
LOK SABHA 
 UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 987 
ANSWERED ON 24.07.2026 
  
NUTRITION DISTRIBUTION AT ANGANWADI CENTRES 
  
987. SHRI RAJKUMAR ROAT:  
 Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a)  the details of the nutrition being provided at Anganwadi Centres in the country, indicating 
the annual budget allocated by the Government therefor and food items being distributed, 
State-wise; 
(b)  the States where the nutrition distribution process is being carried out through Self -Help 
Groups (SHGs) along with the procedure being followed in remaining States and the 
mechanism adopted for quality checking of nutrition in the said States, indicating quality 
check reports for Rajasthan during the last five years; 
(c)  whether earlier nutrition items were prepared and distributed by SHGs whereas currently, a 
contractual system through a tender process has been put in place, which has led to a 
significant decline in quality in Rajasthan, if so, the details thereof; and 
(d)  whether the Government proposes to distribute nutrition items through Self-Help Groups in 
all the States, if so, the details thereof along with the time by which it is likely to be done and 
if not, the reasons therefor?  
  
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR) 
  
(a) to (d):  Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 (Mission Poshan 2.0), 
Supplementary Nutrition is provided to children under 6 years of age, pregnant women, lactating 
mothers and adolescent girls (14 -18 years in Aspirational Districts and North -Eastern region) to 
improve nutritional outcomes. Supplementary Nutrition is provided at all Anganwadi Centres  in 
the country in the form of Take -Home Ration (THR), Morning Snacks and Hot Cooked Meals 

(HCM) to the beneficiaries in accordance with the nutrition norms specified under Schedule-II of 
the National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013.  
The States and Union Territories (UTs) are encouraged to decide menu and recipes suitable to the 
local tastes and conditions and to procure locally grown food items like millets, vegetables, 
condiments, etc. The selection of ingredients, recipes and menu for Supplementary Nutrition rests 
with States and UTs in accordance with local palate and includes locally available cereals/millets, 
pulses, vegetables, nuts and fats. The State -wise details of funds released for the implementation 
of Supplementary Nutrition Programme is at Annexure. 
Mission Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored Mission where the responsibility for implementation 
lies with the respective States and UTs. Accordingly, the States and UTs are free to decide upon 
the model of procurement, including involvement of SHGs in the scheme, in case. The Ministry 
of Women and Child Development (MoWCD), vide notification dated 12th September 2022, 
issued the Integrated Nutrition Support Programme - Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan (2.0), Rules 
2022, to regulate the entitlements specified under the provisions of NFSA, 2013 for every pregnant 
woman and lactating mother, till six months after childbirth and every child in the age group of six 
months to six years. As per these rules, States and UTs have been advised to introduce transparent 
process for procurement as per General Financial Rules, 2017 and applicable Vigilance Guidelines 
and other norms issued from time to time by the Government of India. St ates and UTs also need 
to ensure that THR procured, conforms to nutritional norms set by the Government of India.  
Recently, MoWCD vide letter no. PA/178/2024 -CPMU dated 14 th July 2026, issued the 
Comprehensive Guidelines for Supplementary Nutrition Programme, which emphasize that States 
and UTs to ensure the quality of Supplementary Nutrition being provided to the beneficiaries in 
accordance with the food safety norms. Regular testing through Food Safety and Standard 
Authority of India (FSSAI) recognized laboratories/ National Accreditation Board for Testing and 
Calibration Laboratories (NABL) accredited laboratories is to be conducted. 
As informed by the State of Rajasthan, supply of Supplementary Nutrition from Self Help Groups 
(SHGs) is being done on a pilot basis to five ICDS projects. In remaining 358 ICDS projects of 
the State, supplementary nutrition is being supplied by the Rajasthan State Cooperative Consumers 
Federation Limited (CONFED). Since 2022 –23, all samples of supplementary nutrition supplied 
by CONFED have been found to conform to the prescribed quality standards in NABL laboratory 
testing. Therefore, no decline in quality has been observed by the State authorities.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS 
DEPARTMENT OF FERTILIZERS 
 
LOK SABHA 
 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO.989TO BE ANSWERED ON 24.07.2026 
 
POLICY FOR SAFETY IN AGEING FERTILIZER PLANTS 
 
989: SHRI PARSHOTTAMBHAI RUPALA:  
 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERSbe pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether steps have been taken by the Government regarding safety risks in 
aging fertilizer plants located in densely populated/environmentally sensitive areas 
of the country following the BVFCL Namrup fire, if so, the details thereof, State-
wise; 
 
(b) whether the Government proposes to constitute a High-Level Technical 
Committee to formulate a Strategy for replacing life-expired, obsolete plant 
machinery, if so, the details thereof; 
 
(c) whether there is a proposal to frame uniform national guidelines for phased 
equipment replacement, mandate independent annual safety audits of critical 
machinery and strengthen regulatory compliance accountability, if so, the details 
thereof; and 
 
(d) the steps taken by the Government to reimburse the pending Fixed Cost to 
Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) fertilizer units, which has remained outstanding 
since 2014 as on date, year-wise? 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS 
 
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA) 
 
(a) to (c):The safety and security of urea manufacturing units do not fall directly under 
the purview of the Department of Fertilizers (DoF). However, in order to promote safe 
operations, the Department has developed a model safety protocol checklist, 
obtained from urea units on a monthly basis for review and monitoring. Routine 
health checkup of ammonia systems including storage tanks, adoption of safety in 
design of ammonia storage and handling during transportation, disaster 
management training of employees, emergency response planning are some of the 
major aspects covered in these reports. The mandatory safety audits of Public Sector 
Fertilizer Plants are conducted periodically by the respective Public Sector 
Undertakings (PSUs) through external agencies. Following the fire incidents at 
Brahmaputra Valley fertilizer Corporation Limited (BVFCL),PSUs undertook the  
 

 
-2- 
 
assessment of the incident and initiated necessary corrective and preventive 
measures including inspection of critical equipment in accordance with established 
safety procedure.  
 
Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Limited (BVFCL) has, presently, 
only one operating fertilizer manufacturing plant in Namrup, Assam. BVFCL carry out 
periodic safety audits, inspection of critical equipment, preventive maintenance and 
statuary compliance as per prescribed regulations.  
 
National Fertilizers Limited (NFL) has five gas-based Ammonia-Urea plants 
viz. Nangal & Bathinda plants in Punjab, Panipat plant in Haryana and two plants at 
Vijaipur at District Guna, in Madhya Pradesh. It conducts safety audit of all its 
manufacturing plants every year through Directorate General Factory Advice Service 
and Labour Institutes (DGFASLI) certified Auditor/Agency in accordance with 
Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals (MSIHC) Rules, 1989. 
 
Rashtriya Chemicals & Fertilizers Limited (RCF) has two fertilizer 
manufacturing plants, one at Trombay in Mumbai, Maharashtra and the other at Thal, 
Raigad district, Maharashtra. Apart from regular internal audit through its Safety Audit 
Committees, it conducts safety audit of its manufacturing plants through external 
reputed agencies annually.RCF has implemented Process Safety Management 
(PSM) system as a proactive step to ensure workplace safety. 
 
Madras Fertilizers Limited (MFL) has only one fertilizer manufacturing plant in 
Manali, Chennai, Tamil Nadu. MFL periodically carries out statutory inspections, 
preventive maintenance and safety audits of critical equipment in accordance with 
the applicable statutory provisions and established maintenance practices. 
 
Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore Limited (FACT)has two manufacturing 
plants at Udyogamandal, Kochi, Kerala and at Cochin Division, Kerala. FACT conduct 
internal safety audits through its Safety Audit Committee and engages a reputed 
external agency for audits biennially. 
 
PSUs such as NFL and RCF have been given Navratna status which enabled 
them to have more flexibility in investment by adopting new technologies.  
 
 
(d):  The modified New Pricing Scheme (NPS-III) was notified on 2nd April 2014. 
Thereafter, process to implement the provisions of Modified New Pricing 
Scheme(MNPS-III) was started. Being the implementation agency, Fertilizer Industry 
Coordination Committee(FICC) was compiling/analysing the data. It was observed that 
there is an ambiguity in the approval given by Cabinet Committee on Economic 
Affairs(CCEA). It was proposed to pay a minimum fixed cost of Rs.2300/MT or actual 
fixed cost prevailing during 2012-13, whichever is lower. In other words, no unit shall 
be paid fixed cost more than Rs.2300/MT. Thus Rs. 2300/MT, instead of being a  
 
 

-3- 
 
 
minimum fixed cost i.e. floor, became the ceiling for all fertilizers plants. All the 
confusion arising because of this ambiguity of not clarifying that minimum Fixed Cost 
of Rs.2300/MT was intended only for three units viz., NFL-Vijaipur-I, RCF-Thal and 
KRIBHCO-Hazira. It was never the intention of the Government, Group of Ministers 
and Department of Fertilizers to recover what has already been given to the urea 
industry.  
 
  Thereafter, in October 2018, a CCEA note was prepared to remove the ambiguity 
and Inter-Ministerial Consultation(IMC) was conducted. However, it was decided to 
refer the matter to a Team of Ministers in February 2019. The Team of Ministers gave 
its recommendations in August 2019.  
   
Based on the recommendations of the Team of Ministers, a CCEA note was 
submitted. CCEA approved and deleted the provisions of minimum fixed cost of 
Rs.2300/MT in March 2020.FAI, KRIBHCO-Hazira and NFL represented to the 
Department of Fertilizers to restore the minimum fixed cost of Rs.2300/MT as decided 
in the notification dated 2nd April 2014. A Committee under the chairmanship of 
Additional Secretary and Executive Director, FICC was constituted in September, 
2020 and reconstituted in January 2021 to examine the issue of Minimum Fixed Cost 
of Rs.2300/MT. 
   
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) in December 2022, inter-alia, observed 
that if required, the issues related with costing etc. of the urea units may be referred 
to the Chief Advisor (Cost) in the Ministry of Finance for examination and 
recommendations. Accordingly, the entire gamut of issues related to fixed cost 
including the issue of minimum fixed cost was referred to Chief Advisor Cost (CAC). 
CAC through the Department of Expenditure (DoE) has submitted its report in April 
2025. Subsequently, some meetings have been held between DoF, FICC and CAC. 
Thereafter, meetings were held with Urea units wherein some of the units have raised 
their concerns on the methodology adopted by CAC. The report has been referred to 
NITI Aayog for examination by the Expert Group. 
 
     ***********

(c) whether the Government or the Election Commission has conducted any independent review or 
evaluation of the SIR process to assess its accuracy, transparency and impact on voter enrolment and 
deletion, if so, the details and the findings thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE (INDEPENDENT CHARGE) OF THE MINISTRY OF LAW 
 AND JUSTICE; AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
 PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARJUN RAM MEGHWAL) 
(a): As per the Press Note of the ECI, the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls is being 
carried out in several phases across the country, with the objective of ensuring that the electoral rolls 
are accurate, up -to-date, and free of ineligible or duplicate entries, while ensuring that no eligible 
elector is left out. 
Phase I:  The SIR was first undertaken in the State of Bihar, ahead of the Election s to the State 
Legislative Assembly in the year 2025. The exercise involved house-to-house enumeration by Booth 
Level Officers (BLOs), distribution and collection of enumeration forms, publication of a draft 
electoral roll  and providing a specific period for filing claims and objections, and subsequent 
publication of the final electoral roll after due verification. 
Phase II:  The similar process was followed during Phase -II for nine States and three Union 
territories, namely, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, 
Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and Puduc herry from 
October, 2025 to April, 2026. 

Phase III: The SIR is presently underway or proposed in the remaining States/UTs not covered in 
Phase I and II, including the National Capital Territory of Delhi, in accordance with a schedule 
notified by the ECI, which is subject to revision from time to time based on operational requirements. 
Throughout the exercise, consolidated data on enumeration, additions, deletions, and corrections is 
compiled and published by the ECI on its official website and by the respective Chief Electoral 
Officers of the States/UTs concerned, as the revision progresses. 
(b): As per the Press note of the ECI, t he deletions during SIR are carried out only after due 
verification by Booth Level Officers (BLOs) through house -to-house enumeration, and broadly fall 
under the following categories: (i) death of the elector; (ii) permanent shifting of residence; (iii) 
duplicate entries of the same elector in more than one place; and (iv) electors found untraceable 
despite repeated visits.  
The following safeguards have been put in place by ECI to prevent wrongful deletion of eligible 
electors: 
(i) Prior intimation and door-to-door visits by BLOs, with a minimum of two -three attempts 
before an elector is treated as untraceable; 
(ii) Deletion only after recording reasons in the prescribed enumeration format and following 
the process under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960; 
(iii) Publication of draft electoral rolls and a statutory period for filing claims and objections 
(Forms 6, 7 and 8) before the roll is finalised; 
(iv) Provision for appeal before the District Magistrate/designated appellate authority and 
further recourse to the Chief Electoral Officer; 
(v) Deployment of Booth Level Agents (BLAs) nominated by political parties to verify entries 
and flag discrepancies during the enumeration and claims/objections stages. 
(c): The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in its judgment dated 27.05.2026  in W.P. (C) 6 40 of 2025 titled 
Association for Democratic Reforms & Ors. vs. Election Commission of India & Ors., examined the 
legality of the SIR process and held, inter alia, that the SIR exercise is within the statutory mandate 
of ECI under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and is consonance with the Election 
Commission's constitutional obligation under Article 324 to ensure free and fair elections.  
Further, it is evident from the Press Note of the ECI, that it carries out internal quality checks at each 
stage of SIR, including cross-verification of BLO enumeration through supervisory officers, random 
sample audits of deleted entries, and public disclosure of draft and final rolls to enable scrutiny by 
political parties and electors. Grievances received during the claims and objections period are 
examined and, where found valid, names are restored before finalisation of the roll.
